strengths: LEMON is convincingly the largest open-access surgical video dataset to date (4,194 videos, 938 hours, 85M frames across 35 procedures), substantially exceeding prior public resources (Table 1) and introducing two novel downstream tasks (multi-label procedure type and binary surgery type classification) with a leaderboard.

The multi-stage data curation pipeline (storyboard classification, frame-level trimming, non-surgical content removal via YOLOv8, semi-automatic annotation with manual quality control) is well documented in the supplementary material, with quantitative validation of each stage (e.g., storyboard classifier F1 94.75±1.1, frame classifier F1 95.64±0.94, detection mAP50 79.29±3.4), supporting reproducibility and label quality.

LemonFM is evaluated comprehensively across four downstream tasks and six datasets under both linear probing and full fine-tuning, consistently outperforming existing surgical foundation models (Endo-FM, EndoViT, GSViT, SurgeNetXL) and even specialist architectures, with additional low-data-regime (50% shot) experiments demonstrating data efficiency.

Ablation studies are informative: they isolate the contributions of the dataset vs. ImageNet pretraining (+12.9pp F1 phase recognition), the curation pipeline (+4.5pp F1), and the augmented distillation vs. vanilla DINO (+3.2pp mDice), and compare backbone choices (ConvNeXt vs. ViT) and pretext-task types (generative vs. discriminative).

The proposed augmented distillation idea (using nearest-neighbor cross-patient frames and temporal neighbors as additional supervisory signals in a DINO-style framework) is a sensible, domain-motivated extension for learning invariance to patient appearance variation and surgical motion.

The paper plans to release dataset code, model weights, and download scripts, and addresses licensing (CC BY 4.0), an opt-out mechanism for video authors, and access requests, following established practice for web-scale datasets.
weaknesses: A significant potential confound in the SotA comparisons: LemonFM uses a ConvNeXt-L backbone while several baselines (Endo-FM, EndoViT, GSViT, SurgeNetXL) use ViT-family backbones, and the paper's own ablation shows ConvNeXt-L substantially outperforms ViT-L on segmentation (+10.7pp mDice). Reported gains therefore conflate pretraining data/objective with architecture; a same-backbone comparison with the strongest baseline would strengthen the claims considerably.

The methodological novelty is modest: the augmented distillation is essentially DINO augmented with neighbor-based positives, and the video classification head (typicality-weighted embedding aggregation) is an adaptation of active-learning typicality; neither is a deep technical contribution on its own.

LEMON is sourced entirely from YouTube, whereas downstream evaluation datasets are clinical videos; while the paper argues curation mitigates spurious content, the domain/distribution gap between pretraining data and clinical deployment remains, and title/keyword-based (plus ChatGPT-assisted) procedure annotations may carry label noise despite manual review; the reliability of these weak labels is not quantitatively characterized.

Ethical/licensing concerns are only briefly addressed: redistribution of YouTube surgical footage (potentially identifiable patient content) under CC BY 4.0 and a post hoc opt-out mechanism may not satisfy stricter interpretations of consent and data protection relevant to medical data; a more thorough ethics discussion (and any institutional review) would be appropriate.

Some presentation issues reduce polish: the dataset URL in the abstract is missing, there are typos (e.g., 'surigcal'), and the notation in Eq. 1 (e.g., d(u,v) defined as a log-sum-exp of student outputs) is non-standard and requires careful parsing to map onto the DINO objective.

The comparison in Table 1 mixes metrics sources and concurrent work (SurgeNetXL is a 2025 arXiv preprint), and the leaderboard in Table 6 shows procedure classification remains difficult (57.8% mAP), which the paper acknowledges but does not analyze (e.g., per-class errors or long-tail effects across the 35 procedures).
Only single-seed results (random seed 30) are reported for most downstream experiments; variance estimates (as done for the curation classifiers) would improve confidence in the claimed margins.

strengths: LEMON is a genuinely valuable community resource: at 4,194 videos / 938 hours / 85M frames across 35 procedures it clearly surpasses existing open surgical datasets (Table 1), and the multi-stage curation pipeline (storyboard classification, frame-level trimming, non-surgical content obliteration, semi-automatic annotation with manual QC) is well documented, with classifier performance reported in the supplementary (Tables 1-3, sec. B).

Evaluation breadth is respectable: four downstream tasks across six datasets, under both linear probing and full fine-tuning, plus a 50%-data regime analysis (Tables 2-4) that supports data-efficiency claims.

The ablation studies (Table 5) are a real strength: they isolate the effect of LEMON vs. ImageNet pretraining (+12.9pp F1, +4.3pp mDice), the curation pipeline (+4.5pp F1), and the augmented distillation over vanilla DINO (+3.2pp mDice), and compare ViT vs. ConvNeXt backbones.

Pretraining, data splits, and training hyperparameters are documented in enough detail (supp. C, D) to make the work largely reproducible, and the authors commit to releasing code, annotations, and download links.
weaknesses: Potential pretraining/evaluation data overlap is not addressed. Many of the downstream datasets (Cholec80, M2CAI16, CholecT50, CholecSeg8k, GraSP, AutoLaparo videos) are publicly available on YouTube, and LEMON is scraped from YouTube. The paper never mentions deduplication or verifying that no downstream test videos (or near-duplicates) are in the pretraining set. Given the very large reported gains (e.g., +9.5pp Jaccard on Cholec80), this is a material validity threat that must be quantified, not just asserted away.

Overclaiming relative to the evidence: the abstract states LemonFM 'consistently outperforms' other foundation models across all tasks, yet on frozen-backbone semantic segmentation LemonFM* (71.9 mDice, Table 4) is below EndoViT (73.0). Similarly, linear probing gains are modest on CholecSeg8k. The headline framing does not match the tables.

The large gains conflate multiple factors: pretraining data volume (85M frames vs. ~100K for Endo-FM), curation, and backbone scale. The ablations cover ImageNet-vs-LEMON and DINO-vs-augmented-DINO, but the paper does not disentangle data size from curation (no uncurated-LEMON-at-scale vs. curated-LEMON comparison at equal scale), and ConvNeXt-L is pretrained from scratch while baselines use different architectures/protocols, weakening the comparability of Table 2/3 rows.

The augmented distillation design raises questions: nearest neighbors are selected in the model's own embedding space during training, but the paper does not explain how the embedding space is updated during the 60 epochs (fixed teacher? recomputed each epoch?), nor does it ablate the neighbor-retrieval hyperparameters (cosine-distance threshold 3x, pool size). The ViT-L + augmentation row (61.2 vs 67.4 mDice without aug) suggests the method can be unstable, which is not discussed.

Legal/ethical handling of YouTube medical footage is thin: claiming a CC BY 4.0 license over content the authors do not own is questionable, the opt-out mechanism for original creators is only promised ('We will also provide an online form'), and there is no discussion of patient privacy beyond noting the videos come from public channels. This deserves more careful treatment for a medical dataset.

No statistical rigor: single random seed (30) for pretraining and fine-tuning, no error bars or significance tests on the downstream comparisons, so several claimed margins (e.g., 57.5 vs 57.5/61.9 mAP on CholecT50 vs SurgeNetXL) may not be robust.

Minor but telling presentation issues: the dataset URL in the abstract is empty ('available at .'), Fig. 1 is a hard-to-read radar chart duplicating Tables 3-4, and the LemonFM-Vid typicality-based aggregation (Eq. 2) is introduced with minimal justification and no ablation of K or the weighting scheme.

strengths: LEMON is, by a large margin, the largest open-access surgical video dataset (4,194 videos / 938 hours / 85M frames across 35 procedures, Table 1), addressing a genuine bottleneck in surgical computer vision where prior public datasets are small and single-procedure.

The multi-stage curation pipeline (storyboard classification, frame classification, trimming, non-surgical content obliteration with YOLOv8, manual QC) is well documented, and each curation component is quantitatively validated in the supplementary (94.75% storyboard classifier F1, 95.64% frame classifier F1, 79.29% mAP50 content detector), including five-fold cross-validation.

The ablation studies (Table 5) are meaningful: pretraining on LEMON vs ImageNet-1K (+12.9pp F1 phase recognition), the value of curation (+4.5pp F1), and the augmented distillation vs vanilla DINO (+3.2pp mDice) are all isolated, supporting the paper's core claims about data quality and the pretext task.

Evaluation breadth is respectable: four downstream tasks over six public datasets under both linear probing and full fine-tuning, plus a low-data (50% shot) regime showing data efficiency, and specialist baselines (TeCNO, Trans-SVNet, LoViT) are included alongside foundation models.

Two new downstream tasks (multi-label procedure classification, robotic/non-robotic surgery type) with a leaderboard of strong video models (SlowFast, TimeSformer, MViTv2, Video Swin) provide a useful community benchmark, and the authors honestly note the remaining difficulty (57.8% mAP).

Reproducibility and ethics are addressed seriously: training configurations, splits, hardware, a download/opt-out mechanism for YouTube creators, CC BY 4.0 licensing, and a fair re-evaluation protocol for LemonFM-Vid (retraining from scratch on the accessible training subset).
weaknesses: Comparison fairness / confounds: LemonFM uses a ConvNeXt-L backbone pretrained on ~938 curated hours, while key baselines use smaller backbones and/or smaller or partially private pretraining data (Endo-FM, EndoViT, GSViT, SurgeNetXL). The paper attributes gains to dataset diversity and the distillation method, but the relative contributions of scale, architecture, and method are not fully disentangled (the ViT-L ablation in Table 5 partially helps, but there is no controlled data-scale or backbone-matched comparison against the baselines).

Equation (1), the core proposed loss, is presented incorrectly or at minimum very confusingly: d(u,v) = log Σ exp(σ_k'(f_s(v))) is a log-sum-exp of student logits without a negation or temperature, so minimizing [d(u,v) − n(u,v)] as written does not correspond to the intended distillation cross-entropy (which should be −log σ_argmax(f_t(u))(f_s(v)) with appropriate temperature). This undermines confidence in the technical description of the main methodological contribution.

Reported improvement numbers in the abstract appear inconsistent with Table 3: e.g., AutoLaparo Jaccard 64.8 vs LoViT 55.9 is +8.9pp (claimed +9.5pp), Cholec80 85.1 vs LoViT 81.2 is +3.9pp (claimed +9.4pp), and M2CAI16 79.4 vs Trans-SVNet 74.7 is +4.7pp (claimed +8.4pp). The baselines against which the deltas are computed are not stated and appear to shift across datasets.

Experimental rigor: downstream results are reported for a single random seed (30) without variance or significance testing (five-fold CV is used only for the 50% shot setting), which matters given that several reported margins over the strongest baselines (e.g., SurgeNetXL in tool detection) are moderate.

Notably absent baselines: strong generic self-supervised models such as DINOv2 (or CLIP/SAM features) are not compared, even though the claim 'domain-specific pretraining on LEMON beats general-purpose pretraining' is central — ImageNet-1K MAE/DINO is a weak proxy for modern generic pretraining.

Data limitations and bias are underexplored in the main text: the 500-videos-per-procedure target was not met (4,194 total vs ~18K raw), so procedure prevalence is highly imbalanced (supplementary Fig. 1), and ChatGPT-based title-to-procedure annotation, while manually reviewed, introduces potential label noise whose magnitude is not quantified.

Ethical/privacy treatment, while present (opt-out form, CC BY 4.0), remains a nontrivial concern for republishing identifiable patient footage from YouTube; patient consent cannot be verified and the opt-out mechanism is reactive rather than preventive.

Minor presentation issues: the title's 'MONocular' acronym is strained; some typos ('surigcal', 'ConvNext-B' in Table 5 vs ConvNeXt elsewhere); Table 2 vs Table 3 metrics are not directly comparable without careful reading (frame-level Acc/F1 vs video-level Acc/Jaccard).

strengths: The LEMON dataset is a substantial community contribution: 938 hours / 85M frames across 4,194 videos and 35 procedure types, roughly 40% larger in hours and far more procedurally diverse than the largest prior public datasets (GenSurgery, SurgeNetXL). The curation pipeline (storyboard classification, frame-level trimming, non-surgical region obliteration, semi-automatic annotation with manual verification) is well-motivated and directly addresses a documented weakness of prior web-sourced surgical datasets (Fig. 3).

Evaluation breadth is unusually thorough: four downstream tasks across six independent, hospital-sourced benchmark datasets, under both linear probing (Table 2) and full fine-tuning (Tables 3-4), with consistent gains over Endo-FM, EndoViT, GSViT, and SurgeNetXL (e.g., +9-10pp Jaccard on phase recognition, +10pp mDice on segmentation).

The ablations are informative and support the claims: pretraining on LEMON vs. ImageNet-1K vs. Cholec80 (Table 6), curation vs. no curation (+4.5pp F1), augmented distillation vs. vanilla DINO (+3.2pp mDice), backbone/architecture/pretext-task analysis, threshold and distance-metric sensitivity analyses in the supplement, and 5-fold cross-validation with reported standard deviations (Table 5).

The 50%-shot experiments (Tables 3 and 4) convincingly demonstrate data efficiency, and the computational cost analysis (Table 12) shows the efficiency argument for an image encoder + lightweight temporal head over video-specific models is well supported.

Ethical and legal handling of web-scraped medical data is treated seriously: opt-out mechanisms, link-based removal, human effort accounting (B.6), label reliability via Cohen's Kappa on a stratified subset (B.7), and clear licensing terms. The submission appears highly reproducible with pretraining details, splits, and model variants (CN-B/CN-L) described.
weaknesses: The methodological novelty of the augmented distillation is incremental. The core mechanism—adding nearest-neighbor (same-procedure, cross-patient) and temporally adjacent frames as extra positive views in a DINO-style distillation objective—is a natural combination of DINO with NNCLR-style neighbor mining; the contribution is a sensible domain adaptation rather than a new learning principle.

Some headline gains are large enough to warrant additional scrutiny. E.g., +9.5pp Jaccard over the best specialist and foundation models on AutoLaparo, and Cholec80 Jaccard of 85.1 vs. ~81 for LoViT, are surprising magnitudes. Cross-validation (Table 5) is only performed under linear probing, not for the full fine-tuning results where the largest gains are reported, and single-split results for the strongest competitors partly rely on previously reported numbers (‡ markers), which may embed protocol differences.

The curation pipeline's claimed 100% video-level / >99.9% frame-level precision is based on the authors' own manual review of model-filtered outputs; residual systematic bias from automated filtering (e.g., removal of diagnostically challenging frames such as blood, smoke, blur, which are shown as 'intraoperative scenarios' in Fig. 5 but seemingly kept) is not quantified for its effect on downstream generalization.

There is no explicit check for overlap between LEMON's YouTube-sourced cholecystectomy content and the Cholec80/CholecT50/CholecSeg8k evaluation data (same institutions or public recordings), which could inflate some downstream results; the paper does not discuss this contamination risk.

Procedure/surgery-type ground truth is derived from video titles (with ChatGPT assistance), a weaker annotation source than the frame-level annotations of clinical datasets; Kappa was computed on a 500-video subset, and label noise heterogeneity across procedures is not analyzed.

Presentation issues: the dataset URL in the abstract is blank, Figure 1's radar plot is hard to read (values plotted against axis ticks rather than labeled directly), and the paper does not report per-procedure breakdown of downstream performance, which would substantiate the diversity-benefits claim more directly.

strengths: The LEMON dataset is a substantial and genuinely useful community resource: 4,194 videos / 938 hours across 35 procedure types makes it the largest open-access surgical video dataset (Table 1), and the curation pipeline is unusually well documented, with per-component validation metrics (storyboard classifier F1 94.75%, frame classifier F1 95.64%, detection mAP50 79.29%), a label reliability check via Cohen's Kappa (0.97 for procedure type on 500 videos), and a transparent accounting of human effort (B.6).

The evaluation protocol is comprehensive and largely well-controlled: baselines (MAE, VideoMAEv2) are re-pretrained on LEMON to isolate the data effect, both linear probing and full fine-tuning are reported, a 50%-data regime demonstrates data efficiency, 5-fold cross-validation quantifies stability (Table 5), and ablations cover curation, the proposed distillation, backbone choice, pretext type, and image- vs video-based pretraining (Table 6).

The empirical results are consistently strong across four tasks and six datasets (e.g., +8-10pp Jaccard on phase recognition, 81.3 mDice on CholecSeg8k vs. 71.9 for the next best), and the supplementary ablations justify design decisions such as the 3x cosine-distance threshold and cosine vs. L2 neighbor mining.

Ethical and licensing considerations are addressed more carefully than is typical for web-scraped medical data: opt-out mechanism, CC BY 4.0 license, direct source linking, explicit privacy discussion, and manual removal of patient identifiers.
The paper is clearly written and the pipeline (Fig. 2) and distillation scheme (Fig. 4) are easy to follow; the ChatGPT annotation prompt is disclosed (Fig. 6), aiding reproducibility.
weaknesses: A serious unaddressed validity concern: potential train/test contamination between LEMON and the downstream benchmarks. LEMON contains ~500 cholecystectomy videos collected from YouTube, and footage from the same institutions/procedures that compose Cholec80, CholecT50, and CholecSeg8k circulates publicly online. The paper reports no deduplication, nearest-neighbor overlap analysis, or visual comparison against downstream test splits. Given that the headline gains (e.g., 92.7/85.1 on Cholec80, 81.3 mDice on CholecSeg8k) are the paper's central evidence, this omission is material and could inflate results.

The methodological novelty is modest. The 'augmented distillation' is essentially DINO plus extra positive views drawn from temporal neighbors and cross-video nearest neighbors of the same procedure type — ideas closely related to NNCLR and temporal-contrast approaches. The ablated gain attributable to this component is comparatively small (+3.2pp mDice, Table 6) relative to the gain attributable to data scale and curation, so the paper is primarily a dataset contribution.

Label quality of the newly proposed tasks is questionable: procedure labels come from video titles (ChatGPT-assisted at ~95.2% pre-correction accuracy) and the robotic/non-robotic label is largely keyword matching on titles. The binary surgery-type task appears nearly saturated (98.9% accuracy for two methods, Table 7), and the 35-way classification task's difficulty is entangled with title-derived label noise and anatomically adjacent confusions the authors themselves acknowledge.

Some comparisons are close and unsupported by statistical testing: e.g., M2CAI16 linear probing (68.4 vs. 67.8 for SurgeNetXL) and Cholec80 phase recognition accuracy vs. LoViT (92.7 vs. 92.4). Cross-validation is performed only for LemonFM, not across competing models, so 'statistical testing' claims are not fully substantiated for the main tables.

Licensing and provenance of republishing others' YouTube surgical videos under CC BY 4.0 is legally uncertain; the paper defers to practice on non-medical datasets (ImageNet, Kinetics), which is a weaker argument given patient-privacy sensitivities in surgery. Distribution as download links mitigates but does not eliminate this concern.

Presentation issues: the repository URL in the abstract is a placeholder; citations [17] and [63] (hyperspectral super-resolution, hyperbolic 3D points) appear misplaced in the surgical SSL related-work paragraph, suggesting padding or an error.

The image-vs-video comparison (Sec. 5.3) concludes image models suffice, but VideoMAEv2 is evaluated at ViT-B/16 while LemonFM uses ConvNeXt-L; capacity is not held constant, weakening the temporal-modeling conclusion. Similarly, the ViT vs. ConvNeXt comparison uses DINO-style distillation that is optimized for ViTs, so the +10.7pp segmentation difference may partly reflect objective-architecture mismatch rather than an intrinsic ConvNeXt advantage.

strengths: LEMON is a genuinely large and diverse resource: 4194 videos / 938 hours / 85M frames across 35 procedures, substantially exceeding prior public surgical datasets (Table 1), and it enables two new supervised tasks (procedure type and surgery type classification) with a leaderboard.

The data curation pipeline is systematic and well-documented, with quantified reliability at every stage (storyboard classifier F1 94.75%±1.1, frame classifier F1 95.64%±0.94, >99.9% frame-level precision after review, Cohen's Kappa 0.97 on labels) and an honest accounting of human effort (B.6).

Evaluation is broad and mostly rigorous: four downstream tasks across six datasets, both linear probing and full fine-tuning, external baselines pretrained on the same LEMON data (MAE, VideoMAEv2) to isolate pretraining-data effects, low-data (50% shot) experiments, 5-fold cross-validation for stability, and computational cost analysis (Table 12).

Ablations are informative and incremental: ImageNet vs Cholec80 vs LEMON pretraining, curated vs uncurated data (+4.5pp F1), the proposed augmented distillation vs vanilla DINO (+3.2pp mDice), backbone choice (ConvNeXt vs ViT), and generative vs discriminative pretext tasks are all dissected (Table 6, supplementary C.2).

LemonFM achieves consistent, large improvements over existing surgical foundation models and specialist architectures (e.g., +9.5pp Jaccard AutoLaparo, +8pp Cholec80, >10pp mAP on GraSP, >10pp mDice on CholecSeg8k), and remains ahead even at 50% of downstream labels.
Dataset, code, and models are stated to be publicly released with a defined license and opt-out mechanism, supporting reproducibility and community impact.
weaknesses: Ethical and legal grounding for scraping patient-containing surgical videos from YouTube remains the most fragile aspect. The paper targets 'videos from medical institutions and surgeons' to 'maximize compliance with professional consent standards', but patients in operative footage plausibly did not consent to large-scale ML redistribution; the CC BY 4.0 license and post-hoc opt-out form do not fully address this, and 'patients are, to the best of our knowledge, unidentifiable' is asserted rather than independently verified (e.g., no IRB/ethics-board consultation is reported).

The methodological novelty of LemonFM is modest: the augmented distillation is essentially DINO augmented with nearest-neighbor and temporal views (related to NNCLR-style ideas), and the gains, while real, are relatively small (+3.2pp mDice in the ablation) compared to the gains attributable to data scale and curation.

Potential train/test contamination between LEMON and downstream benchmarks is not explicitly discussed. Although LEMON is YouTube-sourced and benchmarks come from hospitals, some surgical videos and edited hospital recordings do circulate online; an overlap check (e.g., retrieval against downstream test sets) would strengthen the SOTA claims.

Model-capacity fairness is imperfect: LemonFM uses ConvNeXt-L while several compared baselines are ViT-B-scale (e.g., Endo-FM, EndoViT); the ConvNeXt-B variant (Table 12) partially mitigates this, but head-to-head tables mix architectures and some baseline numbers are quoted from prior studies (‡) rather than rerun under the unified protocol.

Minor presentation issues: model selection uses lowest training loss rather than validation loss (C.1); the video-level vs frame-level metric reporting across Tables 2, 3, and 11 takes care to follow; and the abstract's claimed phase-recognition deltas do not always match the exact table margins (e.g., AutoLaparo 85.5/64.8 vs 85.0/55.1 implies ~9.7pp).

Some claims are under-evidenced: the hypothesis that ConvNeXt preserves 'fine-grained surgical details' that ViT patchification collapses is plausible but not directly verified, and the 100% video-level precision claim rests on the authors' own manual review rather than an external audit.
